newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Election turns off British "virgin voters".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Election turns off British "virgin voters".

text.p: Sue Emson has lived all but a few weeks of her life under the same Conservative government.
She's now 18 and eligible to vote in a national British election for the first time.
But far from being filled with fervour for a change of government, she shares the apathy and disillusion with politics felt by many of Britain's so-called "Virgin Voters".

"It seems a shame that we have a vote but there is nothing worth voting for. No one really understands what the politicians are about. They waffle a lot and it all sounds like a petty row," Emson says.
Forty-three percent of under 25-year-olds -- some 2 1/2 million people -- failed to vote in Britain's last election in 1992. Many had not even bothered to register on the electoral roll.
"For many young people, politics has become a dirty word," said Geoff Mulgan, director of the independent think-tank Demos.

"A generation in Britain has opted out of traditional institutions and lost confidence in their ability to tackle the real problems young people face, such as unemployment, homelessness and the environment," he said.

In 1990s Britain, you're more likely to find a young person building a tree house to protest against a new road, or demonstrating against the live export of animals than handing out leaflets for any of the mainstream political parties.
Membership of the Young Conservatives, once seen by the middle-class as the best youth dating agency in Britain with half a million followers, has slumped to 8,000.
POLITICIANS HAVE LOST TOUCH WITH NEXT GENERATION

Politicians are finally waking up to the fact that they have lost touch with the generation that will shape the 21st century and are trying to woo them away from direct action, single issue groups and back into the mainstream.
An all-party campaign with the music industry called Rock the Vote has prompted some 400,000 under 25-year-olds to register to vote in the May 1 election.

The minority Liberal Democrats are sending out political birthday cards to all 18-year-olds and the London nightclub Ministry of Sound is running its own poster and leaflet campaign urging youngsters to use their vote.

"We're doing this because we feel responsible. Clubbing is a huge phenomenon but there is no voice for the thousands of young people who go out every weekend. We want to let them know what an incredible force they can be," said the club's managing director Mark Rodol.
Many young people find the sudden attention patronising and say it smacks of opportunism. But Mulgan is encouraged by the initiatives of the past year.

"I think there is a genuine worry among a lot of politicians of all parties. They are genuinely fearful of a generation completely cut off from politics, they feel they are to blame for this and they want to do something about it," he said.
The opposition Labour Party, more than 20 points ahead in opinion polls, appears to be reaping most of the benefit.

Labour is promising more money for schools and has pledged to create an extra 250,000 jobs for young people. Officials say membership of the party's youth section has more than doubled to 30,000 since Tony Blair took over as leader in 1994.

A recent survey showed that 64 percent of 18-24 year olds -- if they vote at all -- would vote Labour, 23 percent Conservative and eight percent Liberal Democrats. "A lot of young people have seen the same government in power for 18 years. They are disillusioned with a lot of what they see going on in politics and they wonder about the relevance to their lives," said Labour MP Judith Church.
But some of Blair's attempts to appear trendy -- such as presenting a major British pop music award last year -- have not always gone down well.
"It made me cringe," said Tobin Littleford, 18. "It was obvious that the reason for him being there was to attract young votes."

Many students feel there is little to differentiate between Conservative policies and those of Blair's revamped new Labour, which has abandoned some of its historic socialist policies. The Conservatives have been in power since 1979.
"If there was someone you could vote for that you felt would really make a change then I might feel more excited about having the vote for the first time," said 18-year-old James Bartlett.
Liberal Democrat MP Charles Kennedy, 37, acknowledges the fact that the young, with their mixture of cynicism and radicalism, are almost bound to be disappointed.
"When they look at established parties they don't see the degree of radicalism they are looking for, whilst at the same time they are a bit cynical about the lot of us," Kennedy said.
MINORITY PROUD TO BE OUTSIDE THE SYSTEM
A 1995 Demos report said a significant minority of 18-25s took pride in being outside the system.
Taxation and Europe -- the burning issues for most politicians -- cut little ice with the young.

Opinion polls put the environment, animal rights, gay rights and homelessness as their priorities. But Britain's first past the post electoral system means that smaller parties such as the Greens, or single issue groups, have no chance of a seat.

George Monbiot, a prime mover in some of the "direct action" groups that have sprung up on British road building sites in the past year, says the hope encouraged by the Rock the Vote campaign may quickly turn to disillusion.
He urged first timers to vote for small parties "which still uphold some of their ideals".
"In the meantime don't abandon the dugouts. The new voters' pleas may fall on deaf ears but the youthful voice of the underground is coming over loud and clear."
